newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: James Hardie battles soft Australia building scene.
newsitem.headline: James Hardie battles soft Australia building scene.

text.p: Australian based-building products group James Hardie Industries Ltd announced a slide in annual operating profits on Thursday as its buoyant U.S. operations failed to overcome soft Australasian building materials markets.
James Hardie, 28 percent owned by Brierley Investments Ltd, announced a 12.3 percent fall in operating profits to A$51.3 million (US$39 million) for the year to March 31.
Net profit jumped to A$83 million from A$32.2 million in 1995/96 because of a A$31.7 million abnormal profit partly linked to profits from asset sales.

"These results were due mainly to the further 12 percent fall in housing construction in calendar 1996, which had a severe impact on sales volumes and profit margins," managing director Keith Barton said.
But he said the group expected significant improvements in after tax profits in the current 1997/98 year.
"The turn around of underperforming Australian businesses remains a priority while in the United States, we expect strong growth," Barton said.
In the United States, new construction was forecast to remain at or near current high levels and economic and interest rate conditions were expected to remain favourable, he said.
Conditions in the Australian and New Zealand housing markets remained tough with further sales and margins falls, he said.
"The modest recovery in Australian housing construction will not be sufficient to offset the impact of growing competition on our Australian fibre cement business," Barton said.
"Therefore, we expect volumes and earnings from this busienss to decline in the current year," he said.

"In New Zealand, we expect relatively stable market conditions, but a modest decline in sales and profits compared to the strong performance sof recent years, as competition intensifies in major market segments."

Barton said the fundamental transformation of James Hardie in the past year was not fully apparent in the 1996/97 results. He said a wide range of projects had been implemented to cut costs, respond to competition and expand markets.
Sales slipped to A$1.63 billion for the year from A$1.75 billion a year earlier, reflecting divestments during the period. Dividend was unchanged at 13 cents for the year.
Hardie's shares were unchanged at A$4.20 in early trade with the result right in the middle of analysts' expectations.
